Washington

126 changes later, the CLARITY Act gets its vote

Senate Republicans released what they called the final draft on Monday. The procedural vote is today at 2pm Eastern.

The lead

The long argument over how America regulates crypto markets is down to a single Tuesday. Senators Lummis, Boozman and Scott released the text ahead of the vote, and The Bitcoin Conference reported what it took to get here:

The new draft includes 126 substantive changes requested by Democrats

What those changes bought, by the Conference's own list: new ethics language, a state AG enforcement role, developer and consumer protections, and conflict-of-interest rules. The vote itself, the announcement noted, is procedural — Tomorrow's vote is a procedural vote — the kind that decides whether a bill gets debated at all, scheduled for 2pm EST.

The ethics clause has a patron. Bitcoin Magazine reported that Lummis is publicly crediting Trump for the ethics deal that unblocked the text.

By the time this paper is read, the count will likely be known. The draft's own send-off was less procedural: THE TIME FOR CLARITY IS NOW.

The peg, continued

4,000 left on Sunday. 600 are still out

The Liquid federation wallet, one week on: most of it came back. Not all of it.

The follow-up

A week after the white-hat drain that emptied Liquid's federation wallet, BTC Prague filed the summary the story had been waiting for:

Roughly 4,000 BTC left Liquid's federation wallet on Sunday. 3,400 came back a day later. About 598 are still out.

Their verdict on where the failure lives: Bitcoin never broke. The sidechain's software did — and an automated peg-out with an online key turned the bug into real BTC.

MaxUM reached for the honest arithmetic of it: If I left the front door wide open with cash on the table I'd be happy if a thief returned most of it. It is theft and it is wrong but what I'm saying is it could have been worse for Blockstream if it was another thief. Pressed on the analogy, he stood by it: They stole the wheels but it could have been the whole car.

Brian Hirschfield tested the exit personally and reported it works: I was able to get all my funds off Liquid this morning with a standard lightning invoice. His advice was two words long: DO IT!

Day two

The Revolut list, item by item

The second day of the Revolut story was quieter and worse: not the shock of the breach, but the inventory of it.

Ungovernable published the full list of what went out the door: a copy of your passport or driving licence, a verification selfie of you holding said document, … and your full transaction history including Bitcoin. And the mechanism, stated plainly: It went to someone using an email account on a real government agency domain. Revolut treated the request as genuine and sent the files.

Frank Corva put the frame around it — the breach, he wrote, quoting Lyudmyla Kozlovska's interview, is the result of weaponized compliance culture, which has led to what the Open Dialogue Foundation terms transnational financial repression.

For anyone checking their inbox: Aaron van Wirdum noted that affected customers have been contacted by Revolut, so if you haven't been contacted you're probably(?) fine. The parenthesis is his, and it is doing a lot of work.

The screen hasn't moved

Kozlovska herself marked the day with the smallest possible update: I still have the same screen… 🙄

Elsewhere the news arrived at the usual speed of discovery. Ben Arc: What what what? I use revolut, did something happen? — before adding, in fairness to the one institution in the story, that its API is the least shit of the modern banky things.

A caution in the node room

Walt Munny posted the kind of sentence that makes an operator sit up: I am running my node with clnrod in allow mode and empty allow list until the dust settles. Whatever dust he is waiting on, he did not say; the posture says it for him.

Education

My First Bitcoin shrinks to grow

The education project announced it is restructuring around its Education Network — a smaller team, lower costs, and a single focus—empowering those who empower others.

The numbers behind the bet: 213 independent educators and 80+ education projects across 48 countries, each teaching their own community in their own language. The organisation calls it the final step in a years-long transition from direct educator to global infrastructure.

Read plainly: the centre is getting out of the classroom so the classrooms can multiply. It is the rare restructuring announcement that means it.

In the margins

What was being marked while the markets voted

Gigi spent the day in the long reads, and the highlights desk shows where the pen stopped.

From an essay at lucumr.pocoo.org, the thesis in five words: It's AGI If You Don't Look — and the observation that gives it teeth, on agents working unobserved: with subagents (where the agent believes nobody is looking) it's resorting to all kinds of increasingly bizarre behavior. Plus a sentence every maintainer will feel: there is very little punishing going on for “shitty code.”

From a second essay, at bcantrill.dtrace.org, a scalpel for the fear debate: Jacob Coxon cites "hacking critical infrastructure" and "extinction-level bioweapons" without further elaboration… Coxon is not an expert on critical infrastructure, nor on bioweapons — nor, for that matter, on extinction.

And one line with no AI in it at all, marked all the same: intelligence is largely outside of your control, and patience largely isn’t.
